newsitem.title: BOSNIA: NATO says decision soon on follow-on force.
newsitem.headline: NATO says decision soon on follow-on force.

text.p: NATO leaders on Thursday said the alliance will not abandon Bosnia after the mandate of its current mission expires in December and that a decision on a follow-up force would be made soon.

NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana and the Supreme Allied Commander Europe, U.S. General George Joulwan, declined to discuss plans for a follow-on force during a visit to the Bosnian capital Sarajevo.
Solana indicated NATO troops would remain in Bosnia after the current peacekeeping mandate runs out on December 20 but said no final decision had been made.
"NATO will not abandon Bosnia," he told a news conference.
He said the North Atlantic Council would be taking up the issue soon and that a final decision would be made in "coming weeks".
"Alliance military authorities are considering different options. We will start discussing those options in the council in Brussels in coming days," he said.
NATO was sent in last December to monitor peace after the three sides signed an acoord in Paris.
U.S. President Bill Clinton promised a hostile Republican-dominated Congress he will pull out some 20,000 American troops in the force by the end of 1996.
Western allies said they would also pull out if the Americans went but Solana confirmed that Germany had pledged to contribute troops to any future mission in Bosnia.
NATO chiefs also held talks with the three members of Bosnia's peacetime collective presidency at the airport. Solana said the talks were "positive" but offered few other details.
Solana and Joulwan flew into Sarajevo to attend a ceremony marking the transfer of command for the Bosnia peace force.
U.S. Admiral Joseph Lopez handed over command of the implementation force (IFOR) to U.S. General William Crouch at the ceremony held at Sarajevo airport.
Lopez, IFOR's second commander since alliance troops deployed last December, served for three months.
Lopez said in a speech the peace force had been a success so far but expressed concern over violations of an arms control agreement signed by Moslem, Croat and Serb armies.
The admiral's comments coincided with reports from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) on Thursday which accused Bosnian Serbs of violating the regional arms control pact.
The arms agreement was agreed in Florence in June after six months of negotiations mediated by the OSCE.
During Lopez's tenure, IFOR troops provided security for the country's sensitive national elections in September which went ahead without any serious violence.
General Crouch will be taking over at the end of IFOR's one- year mandate but NATO sources say he will almost certainly be presiding over a follow-on force in 1997.
IFOR's mission would "remain focused on the implementation of the provisions of the Dayton peace accords and particularly upon the protection of our forces," Crouch said in a speech.
Crouch, commander of Allied Land Forces Central Europe, commanded calvary troops during the Vietnam war and most recently served as chief of staff for U.S. forces in South Korea.
